positions/christus-victor/oneLine: In Christ God himself enters the battle against the tyrants that hold humanity — sin, death, the devil and the powers — and through the cross and resurrection triumphs over them and sets creation free.
positions/christus-victor/coreClaims/0: The human plight is bondage to hostile powers, not only guilt.
positions/christus-victor/coreClaims/1: Atonement is God’s own continuous work from first to last, not an offering from below.
positions/christus-victor/coreClaims/2: The cross and resurrection form one victory: death is "trampled down by death".
positions/christus-victor/coreClaims/3: The victory is applied as liberation, new life and participation in Christ’s triumph.
positions/christus-victor/origin: Named by Gustaf Aulén (Christus Victor, Swedish 1930, English 1931), who argued it was the dominant view of the New Testament, the fathers and Luther; deeply rooted in Eastern Orthodox paschal liturgy.
positions/christus-victor/strongestArgum: It reflects the dominant patristic and liturgical imagery, especially of Easter.
It integrates resurrection and cosmic redemption.
It resonates in cultures attentive to spiritual powers (much of Africa, Asia and Latin America).
positions/christus-victor/strongestObjec: It is less clear about how the victory deals with guilt and the justice of God.
Critics say Aulén’s historical typology oversimplifies the fathers and Luther, both of whom also used penal and sacrificial language.
The "mechanism" of victory can remain vague.
positions/christus-victor/responses/0: Proponents answer that it is a motif, not a mechanism, and can include forgiveness as liberation from sin’s dominion.
positions/christus-victor/responses/1: Many now argue for Christus Victor as the overarching frame within which substitution functions.
positions/christus-victor/consequences/0: Revived across denominations after 1931; influential in Pentecostal spiritual-warfare piety and Anabaptist theology.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/oneLine: Human societies contain rivalrous violence by uniting against scapegoats; the Gospels tell the story from the innocent victim’s side, unmasking and ending sacred violence, so the cross saves by exposing rather than satisfying violence.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/coreClaims/0: Human desire is mimetic and leads to rivalry and violence.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/coreClaims/1: Archaic religion channels this violence onto a scapegoat, whose death restores peace and is then sacralised.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/coreClaims/2: The Bible progressively sides with victims; in the Passion the mechanism is fully revealed.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/coreClaims/3: God does not demand the victim; humans do. Christ’s forgiveness breaks the cycle.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/origin: René Girard (Violence and the Sacred, 1972; Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World, 1978; I See Satan Fall Like Lightning, 1999), developed theologically by Raymund Schwager, James Alison and S. Mark Heim.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/strongestArg: It offers a powerful anthropology linking the cross to the persistence of scapegoating violence.
It explains why the Gospels emphasise Jesus’ innocence and the crowd’s unanimity.
It removes any suggestion that God requires violence.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/strongestObj: It may make sin chiefly social violence and neglect guilt before God.
Many anthropologists dispute the universality of the scapegoat mechanism.
Evangelicals argue it cannot account for texts where God "laid on him the iniquity of us all".
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/responses/0: Girardians answer that "sin" in Scripture is profoundly bound up with violence and idolatry.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/responses/1: Girard himself later allowed a reinterpreted sense of "sacrifice" as self-giving love.
positions/mimetic-scapegoat/consequences: Influential in peace theology, restorative justice and literary studies.
positions/nonviolent-atonement/oneLine: God does not require or will the violent death of Jesus; the cross is the result of the powers’ rejection of the reign of God, and God saves by the resurrection’s victory and by Christ’s nonviolent faithfulness.
positions/nonviolent-atonement/coreClaim: Atonement models that make violence God’s instrument misrepresent the God revealed in Jesus.
Jesus’ death is the consequence of his confrontation with the powers.
The resurrection is God’s victory and vindication.
Salvation means joining Jesus’ nonviolent reign of God.
positions/nonviolent-atonement/origin: Proposed by J. Denny Weaver (The Nonviolent Atonement, 2001), drawing on Anabaptist ethics, Black and womanist theology (Delores Williams), and feminist critiques such as Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker (1989).
positions/nonviolent-atonement/strongest: It coheres with Jesus’ teaching on nonviolence and love of enemies.
It responds to pastoral concerns that atonement theology has been used to justify abuse and passive suffering.
It recovers the narrative and political dimensions of the Gospels.
It struggles with texts of the Father "giving up" the Son (Rom 8:32; Isa 53:10).
Critics argue it confuses God’s judgement on sin with human violence.
Orthodox and evangelical critics see it as reducing atonement to ethics.
positions/nonviolent-atonement/responses: Proponents answer that God "giving up" the Son means sending him into a violent world in love, not inflicting violence.
They point to the early church’s pacifism and Christus Victor imagery as precedent.
positions/nonviolent-atonement/consequen: Influential in peace churches, progressive evangelicalism and feminist theology.
positions/participatory-union-atonement/: Participatory / union atonement
vicarious humanity of Christ
interchange
incarnational atonement
ontological atonement

Atonement takes place within the person of Christ: by assuming our humanity, living, dying and rising as its representative, he includes us in himself, heals and reconciles human nature from within, and brings us into the Son’s communion with the Father by the Spirit.
"What is not assumed is not healed": the incarnation is itself atoning.
Christ acts as our representative and substitute in his whole life — faith, obedience, worship, repentance — not only in his death.
Believers are saved by sharing in Christ ("in Christ", "with Christ"): his death is our death, his life our life.
Atonement is both forensic and ontological, filial rather than merely legal.

Colossians 3:1-4

Rooted in Irenaeus, Athanasius and Gregory of Nazianzus; renewed by John McLeod Campbell (1856), Karl Barth, T. F. Torrance (The Mediation of Christ, 1983; Atonement, 2009) and J. B. Torrance; in New Testament studies by Morna Hooker’s "interchange" (1971) and Michael Gorman.
Morna Hooker
Michael Gorman
Douglas Campbell
Colin Gunton
It takes the pervasive Pauline "in Christ" and "with Christ" language as central.
It holds incarnation, cross, resurrection and ascension together.
It grounds assurance and worship in Christ’s own response to the Father rather than in our faith.
Critics say it can blur Creator and creature or make atonement automatic for all humanity.
Reformed critics argue that Campbell and the Torrances weaken penal substitution and the wrath of God.
Questions remain about the role of personal faith if humanity is already included in Christ.
Proponents reply that they affirm substitution, reframed within the vicarious humanity of the Son.
They distinguish the objective inclusion of humanity in Christ from its subjective realisation by the Spirit through faith.
Shapes Scottish and Torrance-influenced Reformed theology, Trinitarian "union" movements and ecumenical dialogue with Orthodoxy.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/oneLi: Infants are to be baptised because baptism is God’s gift of new birth, forgiveness of (original) sin and incorporation into Christ’s Church, received in the faith of the Church and of parents and godparents.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/coreC: Baptism truly effects what it signifies: regeneration, cleansing from original sin and adoption.
Grace precedes any human response, so infants are fitting recipients.
Infants are baptised in the faith of the Church, voiced by parents and godparents, to be personally professed later.
In the Eastern churches infants are baptised by triple immersion, chrismated and communicated at once.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/origi: Practised by c.200 (Tertullian, Origen, Hippolytus); defended by Cyprian (c.253) and Augustine (412) against Pelagius; universal in East and West by the early Middle Ages; retained by Lutherans and Anglicans.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/propo: Gregory of Nazianzus (counselled delay till about three unless danger)
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/stron: It expresses the priority of grace: God acts before we can respond.
It stands in unbroken practice from at least the late second century, attested as apostolic tradition by Origen.
Jesus welcomed children and the promise is "to you and to your children" (Acts 2:39).
Believers’ baptists: the New Testament pattern is repentance and faith before baptism; no infant baptism is clearly recorded.
Tertullian already counselled delay, and many fourth-century saints (Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom) were baptised as adults.
Mass infant baptism produced nominal Christendom.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/respo: Paedobaptists answer that household baptisms and the covenant pattern imply children; adult baptisms in the 4th century reflect delay, not denial.
They argue that faith is nurtured within the Church after baptism, completed in confirmation/chrismation and personal confession.
positions/paedobaptism-sacramental/conse: Made baptism coextensive with membership in Christian society for over a millennium.
Defended against Anabaptists by both Trent and the magisterial Reformers.
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/oneLin: The children of believers are members of the covenant of grace and should receive its sign and seal, as Israel’s sons received circumcision; baptism does not automatically regenerate but signifies and seals God’s promise, which the Spirit applies in his time.
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/coreCl: There is one covenant of grace in Old and New Testaments; baptism replaces circumcision as its sign (Col 2:11-12).
God’s promise is "to you and to your children" (Acts 2:39); children of a believer are "holy" (1 Cor 7:14).
The efficacy of baptism is not tied to the moment of administration but to God’s promise received by faith.
Baptised children are to be raised as members of the Church and called to personal faith.
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/origin: Formulated by Zwingli (Of Baptism, 1525) and Bullinger against the Anabaptists, developed by Calvin (Institutes IV.16, 1559), the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Q. 74) and the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 28).
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/strong: It reads the Bible as one covenant story in which households and children are included.
It honours the continuity of God’s dealings with families.
It avoids both sacramental automatism and individualism.
Baptists: the new covenant is made with those who know the Lord (Jer 31:34); its sign belongs to regenerate believers.
Circumcision was a sign of ethnic and national membership that the New Testament replaces with Spirit-wrought faith.
Sacramental paedobaptists: it weakens what baptism actually does.
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/respon: Reformed paedobaptists answer that the new covenant community still contains a visible/invisible distinction (Heb 6; Rom 11).
They reply to sacramentalists that baptism is truly a means of grace, though grace is not bound to its moment (Westminster 28.6).
positions/paedobaptism-covenantal/conseq: Shaped Reformed family religion, catechising and the debate over "covenant children".
Recast by Methodists within a Wesleyan framework of prevenient grace.
